opus-5.5.text:
Compute has some unusual properties that make it a much better chokepoint than most dual-use inputs.

First, the supply chain is extraordinarily concentrated. If you trace a cutting-edge AI chip back, you find a handful of companies at each critical step. TSMC fabricates essentially all of the leading-edge logic. ASML is the only company that makes the EUV lithography machines needed for those nodes. NVIDIA dominates the design side, and a small number of firms supply high-bandwidth memory. Compare that to biology: the equipment for synthesizing or manipulating pathogens is relatively cheap, widely distributed, and getting cheaper. Benchtop DNA synthesizers, standard lab gear, knowledge in papers. There's no single fab you can watch.

Second, chips are physical, and at the frontier you need a lot of them. Training a frontier model isn't one GPU in someone's basement. It's tens of thousands of accelerators, huge power draw, specialized cooling, and datacenter infrastructure. That's hard to hide. You can see it, sometimes from satellites, and you can see the electricity. It's more like enriched uranium than like code. Software and model weights, once they exist, can be copied at essentially zero marginal cost. The hardware can't.

Third, the chips themselves can carry governance mechanisms. People have proposed hardware-level features like location verification, tamper-evident modules, or attestation that a chip is running in an approved cluster. You can't really do that with a centrifuge or a chemical precursor in the same way. Compute is programmable, so in principle it can help enforce rules about its own use.

Fourth, it's hard to replicate the manufacturing base. Building a competitive leading-edge fab takes years, tens of billions of dollars, and tacit knowledge accumulated over decades. Even well-resourced states trying to catch up have struggled to match the frontier. That gives export controls real teeth, at least for a while, in a way that controls on, say, dual-use chemicals often don't.

That said, I don't want to overstate it. There's smuggling, there are cloud access loopholes where someone rents compute they couldn't buy, there's stockpiling ahead of controls, and algorithmic efficiency keeps improving, so what counts as "dangerous compute" keeps shrinking. Compute governance buys you leverage and time. It's not a permanent solution. But among the levers we have, it's probably the most tractable one. It's the closest thing AI has to fissile material, and nonproliferation worked in nuclear partly because fissile material was hard to produce and easy to track.

r001.rationale: The response describes a concentrated supply chain and names TSMC, ASML, and NVIDIA, but it does not identify their concentration in Western countries and allies.

r002.rationale: It says building a competitive leading-edge fab takes years, tens of billions of dollars, and decades of tacit knowledge, and that states have struggled to catch up—making domestic replication a barrier to circumventing controls.

r003.rationale: The response compares compute to fissile material and discusses nuclear nonproliferation, but does not judge manufacturing cutting-edge GPUs to be harder than making nuclear weapons.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the key thing is that compute is really unusual among dual-use inputs because it's extremely concentrated at the supply chain level. If you look at cutting-edge AI chips, basically all of them are designed by a handful of companies, mostly Nvidia, and they're fabricated by TSMC, and the lithography machines come from ASML. So you have these chokepoints where there are maybe three or four organizations in the entire world that you'd need to coordinate with. That's just not the case for, say, biology, where the inputs are things like DNA synthesizers and reagents and knowledge that's widely distributed, or something like chemistry where precursors are spread all over the place and have a lot of legitimate uses.

The other thing is that these chips are physical, they're expensive, and they're countable. A frontier training run needs tens of thousands of these GPUs, which is billions of dollars of hardware sitting in a data center that draws a huge amount of power. You can't really hide that. It's not like a piece of software that can be copied for free or a file you can email. So you can actually track where they go, you can put in export controls, and in principle you could put features on the chips themselves, like on-chip mechanisms for location verification or usage reporting, so that if they end up somewhere they shouldn't be, they stop working or at least you know about it.

So it's not that it's a perfect lever. There's smuggling, there's the question of how long the lead lasts before other countries develop domestic alternatives, and so on. But compared to the other inputs to catastrophic capabilities, which are algorithms and data, which are basically free to copy and proliferate instantly, compute is the one input that's rivalrous, scarce, and goes through a very narrow pipe. That makes it the most tractable thing to govern. I'd say it's the closest thing we have to enriched uranium in this domain, in the sense that controlling the physical input is a lot more feasible than controlling the knowledge.

r001.rationale: It describes a supply chain concentrated among a few companies and organizations, but does not identify those chokepoints as being in Western countries and their allies.

r002.rationale: It mentions that other countries may develop domestic alternatives, but does not say that reproducing the entire cutting-edge GPU supply chain domestically is difficult.

r003.rationale: It compares controlling compute to controlling enriched uranium, but does not judge manufacturing cutting-edge GPUs harder than making nuclear weapons.

astra-6.text:
I think the key difference is that cutting-edge GPUs depend on a very concentrated supply chain. There are relatively few companies that can design them, manufacture them, or produce the equipment needed to manufacture them. So there are chokepoints where restrictions can actually be enforced.

With some other dual-use technologies, the inputs are widely available and have a huge range of ordinary uses. It’s much harder to restrict those without disrupting a lot of legitimate activity. Advanced chips are also dual-use, but producing competitive substitutes requires enormous capital investment and specialized expertise. You can’t easily recreate that manufacturing capability in a garage.

That doesn’t mean restrictions are airtight. There can be smuggling, access through cloud providers, and improvements that let people do more with older hardware. But if you need a large number of cutting-edge GPUs to train a frontier system, restricting access can meaningfully raise the cost and slow things down. It’s a more tractable point of control than many other inputs.

r001.rationale: The response says the supply chain is concentrated among relatively few companies, but does not place that concentration in Western countries and their allies.

r002.rationale: It says recreating manufacturing capability requires enormous capital and expertise, but does not clearly identify reproducing the entire supply chain domestically as the barrier.

r003.rationale: The response does not compare GPU manufacturing with making nuclear weapons.

sol-6.1.text:
The key difference is how concentrated the supply chain is. Cutting-edge GPUs are extraordinarily difficult to manufacture. You need advanced fabrication facilities, specialized equipment, and a great deal of capital. There are relatively few companies involved, which creates chokepoints where restrictions can actually be enforced.

Compare that with biology, where many of the tools and materials have legitimate uses across thousands of laboratories, and some capabilities are becoming cheaper and more widely distributed. With advanced compute, you have a much smaller number of suppliers to monitor, and training a frontier model requires a large concentration of those chips.

That doesn’t mean restrictions are airtight. You can have smuggling, intermediaries, or access through cloud providers. But you don’t need perfect enforcement for a restriction to matter. Increasing the cost and difficulty of assembling a very large compute cluster can meaningfully slow access to the most powerful capabilities.

r001.rationale: It says relatively few companies are involved, but does not identify the supply chain as concentrated in Western countries and their allies.

r002.rationale: It describes GPU manufacturing as difficult and capital-intensive, but does not say that reproducing the entire supply chain domestically is a barrier to circumventing restrictions.

r003.rationale: It does not compare the difficulty of manufacturing cutting-edge GPUs with making nuclear weapons.
